A string holds only the brackets ( ) [ ] { }. Decide whether it's balanced: every opening bracket is closed by the same kind of bracket, and a bracket opened later is closed first.

"{[()]}" is balanced. "([)]" isn't: the [ is closed after the ( it contains was left open. "((" isn't either: two brackets never close.

The Key Idea

The last bracket you opened is the first one that must close. "Last in, first out" is exactly what a stack does.

  • On an opening bracket, push it.
  • On a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its partner. Pop it; if it isn't the partner, or the stack is empty, the string is invalid.
  • At the end, the stack must be empty: an opening bracket left on it never closed.

The Solution

def is_balanced(text):
    partner = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []
    for char in text:
        if char in partner:
            if not stack or stack.pop() != partner[char]:
                return False
        else:
            stack.append(char)
    return not stack

Step by Step

With "{[()]}":

Character Action Stack after
{ Push {
[ Push { [
( Push { [ (
) Pop (, matches { [
] Pop [, matches {
} Pop {, matches empty

The stack ends empty, so the string is balanced. With "([)]", the ) pops a [, which doesn't match: invalid.

Complexity

One pass over the string: O(n) time. The stack can hold every character when they're all opening brackets: O(n) extra space.

Common Mistakes

  • Counting instead of stacking. Counting each kind catches "((" but not "([)]", where every count is balanced and the order is wrong.
  • Popping an empty stack. A string starting with ) must return false, not crash: check the stack before popping.
  • Forgetting the end. "((" never hits a mismatch. Only the final "is the stack empty?" check catches it.
